Spent the last week reading every study I could find on whether running wearables can predict injury.

Short answer: they can't, and the evidence against it is much stronger than the industry lets on.

Thread on what I found

The definitive paper is Bahr 2016 in BJSM. To validate an injury screening test you need three things. Nobody has ever cleared the third.

His conclusion: "there is currently no example of a screening test for sports injuries with adequate test properties."

Ruddy 2018 tested the three best-known hamstring injury risk factors with ML on elite AFL players.

Median AUC 0.58. Between-year prediction: 0.52.

That's a coin flip.

ACWR -- the workload metric the entire industry runs on -- got a proper RCT.

34 teams. 482 players. 10 months.

No difference in injury rates.

Here's the one that surprised me most. GRF impact metrics -- what your wearable calls "impact load" -- don't track actual tibial bone load.

Impact peak: r = -0.29. Loading rate: r = -0.20.

Negative. 76 of 80 subject correlations pointed the wrong way.

But there IS something that works, and it isn't prediction.

Chan et al. 2018, AJSM. 320 novice runners. Two weeks of gait retraining with real-time feedback. 12-month follow-up.

Injury rate: 16% vs 38%. HR 0.38.

The pattern across everything I read:

What works is the intervention, not the identification.

Nobody has ever shown that screening *who* gets the intervention beats just giving it to everyone.

If you're a runner who has tried changing your form -- deliberately, with any kind of feedback -- I'd genuinely like to hear whether it stuck.

Building something in this space, and the honest version looks very different from what's on the market.
